strengths: Teacher selection for language-model distillation is relevant to efficient NLP. The GPT-2 and Pythia experiments systematically explore multiple teacher sizes and pruning ratios using both perplexity and downstream accuracy.

MiniMA provides useful practical evidence. It outperforms several similarly sized baselines, and Table 4 reports improvements over the no-distillation variant on all six benchmarks, including GSM8K (8.11 versus 5.08) and HumanEval (10.98 versus 8.54).

The manuscript describes the pruning procedure, training objective, data mixtures, major hyperparameters, hardware, and evaluation settings, and provides code and checkpoint links. These are valuable foundations for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The experiments do not isolate capacity gap from student construction. In Section 3.2, each student is pruned from its corresponding teacher, so changing teacher size also changes inherited weights, pruning severity, and potentially student architecture at comparable parameter counts. Pruning damage and architectural differences remain alternative explanations for the observed optimum. Controls that hold student architecture and initialization fixed while varying teachers are needed to support the general teacher-selection claim.

The proposed law T ≈ 2.5S is insufficiently validated. The manuscript does not adequately explain how fixed-student optima are extracted from the unequal student sizes in Figure 5, or report fit uncertainty, repeated runs, and predictive accuracy on held-out configurations. Appendix B's data-scale evidence compares only 90% and 100% checkpoints from the same training runs. The 7B-versus-13B comparison supports one local observation but does not establish the predicted optimum. Broader training budgets and nearby teacher sizes should be tested, or the claim narrowed to a pipeline-specific heuristic.

The headline compute-efficiency comparison omits a substantial required training stage. Appendix C adapts the 7B teacher for one epoch on the 126B-token mixture, whereas Appendix A counts only student distillation. Using the paper's own approximation, adaptation adds about 5.3 × 10^21 FLOPs to the reported 4.0 × 10^21, yielding approximately 9.3 × 10^21 before pruning overhead. Even treating original teacher pretraining as a sunk cost, this omission materially changes the comparison. A compute-matched direct-training control and an explicit accounting boundary are needed.

Several categorical interpretations exceed the evidence. Table 1's resource estimates for two existing approaches do not establish an 'impossible triangle,' and benchmark gains from one selected teacher do not independently validate the proposed law. The paper should distinguish observed behavior, empirical extrapolation, and impossibility claims.

The MiniChat evaluation has additional reliability and reporting limitations. GPT-4 version, response-order controls, and human-assessment sample sizes are unspecified; Appendix M incorrectly interprets Spearman correlation 0.54 as 54% consistency. Appendix K acknowledges unresolved benchmark contamination. The supposedly successful coding example in Table 15 also returns the first array when the second is empty, producing an incorrect intersection. These issues weaken the application evidence. Together with the central experimental confounding and incomplete compute accounting, they warrant targeted revisions and new controls before a Findings recommendation.
